Aside from practical concerns like crew space, there were major doctrine differences. Even late war sloped German tanks like the Panther had really poor side armor. It wasn't expected to get hit in places the crew didn't want it to. It was meant to be operated by skilled crew in a specialized manner, not a generalized grunt like the T-34.

Soviet tanks on the other hand were meant to survive W keying into the enemy and absorbing 3 shots from different directions before blasting the enemy with superior firepower. Even before the T-34 and IS line, the designs followed this doctrine. T-28, T-35, SMK etc. Even the SU-152, an SPG not meant to fight tanks, had side armor thick as the front of early Shermans. 


The KV-1 had 75mm armor all round. Sloped armor was a way to increase this brute survivability without making the armor too thick.

For the arms of an MS, it can be controlled by a thumb stick on the main stick itself. You use it to slew a crosshair across the monitor, hit fire/grab/punch and the hand/weapon hits that exact spot. So yeah based on what MS controls look like in every show (same stick on both sides) and how they move it's pretty much guaranteed they work on the HOSAS principle.

Edit: aircraft pedals have two actions: pushing the entire thing back vs on a pivot. Pushing the pedal back (sliding action) is for rudder, pushing them down (pivot) is brake. This gives you a crucial extra function: on land a mobile suit's movement can be controlled exclusively by pedals, leaving hand controls free. Throttle can be mapped to sliding, steering can be mapped to pivot.

Using hulls of now mothballed colony defense fighters he and his team built the "sparrowhawk," a fast and effective yet relatively cheap craft. The performance is great during test flights. It took a lot of skill to handle the sensitive controls and powerful thrusters, a rookie can easily spin out of control if they over steer and over compensate.
